title: Audition at the Marigold and first night with the Owls at the Roosevelt
summary: Frank describes a 46-tune audition, a 30 dollar a week job, and being asked to sub for the Owls at the Roosevelt; non-union rule, borrowing a trombone, Halloween night, Earl Crumb offering the job.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Yeah, well, he liked to get an extra $75 to go to have his wife have his first child. And so we went up there and played an audition, I don't remember the fellow's name, but and he says how many, we played several tunes for him over there, Ain't She Sweet and those kind of tunes which was popular in those days, and the guy, and I was playing trumpet, and I went out there and the guy said how many tunes do you know? He says, I said well we can write down and we'll play 46 tunes for you. I didn't know we were at 46 or not, he said well it'd be 46 before you repeat one, you know, you play two choruses and they'd collect the dance, the Ten Cents to Dance, and then then as soon as you see them all walk off the floor there, you'd sort the next tune and play two choruses, I would do you remember that Godfrey over there from the fine. And so we took the job for two weeks. Then he wanted to keep us the third week, but before I said no, and I said I want to go. Well around the second week there, Al Streeman come over there and he spoke to me, he says, I said would you be interested to play a night in a hotel next week, in the Roosevelt Hotel? And I said with the Isles Orchestra, I never heard of the Isles Orchestra, I didn't know anything about them. And I said well how much do they pay? He says ten dollars. I said ten dollars? We were getting thirty bucks a week to play seven days a week down there. And I said ten dollars? I said yeah I'll take it. So I went over there and Bill Padron got his tooth pulled and I played the night for him. And Al Crumb come to me and he says, you know we're non-union. And he says we have an agreement with the boss over here, which was Mike Moss running the Roosevelt at the time. And he says that as long as you stay non-union you'll have a job. But if you join the union, out you go. So he says we'd like to add a trombone to the band. I said well, I said I played trombone in the service. I said, he said well can you get a horn? I went to the Boyle Islands and borrowed it from Brownlee, you remember Brownlee, Godfrey? I borrowed it from Brownlee and I told him, I said look, I said if I take the job, I said I'll buy a horn for you. So he loaned me the horn and I went to play there, it was Halloween night. The year, I don't know whether it was, you remember what year it would be? 25, 26?
This was before the Owls recorded?

No, they made one recording. Pardon me for interrupting you for just a second, these names came to my mind just now. Warren Herron was the drummer with Johnny Tobin's band and Bonnie Pottle was the bass player. Yeah, that's right, Bonnie Pottle.
In fact he worked with us when I was with him at the Edgewater Beach Hotel. Yeah, Bonnie Pottle. In 1940. In fact I think he committed suicide. So go ahead, I'm sorry, Bonnie Pottle.

Yeah, yeah, Halloween night. And Mike Moss, he's big up there with his glass eye. I didn't know he had a glass eye. And when you look at a glass eye, it's always looking at you, you know? So I thought it was looking at me all the time. So Earl Crumb, after the night was over the next day, he says, well, the job is yours. He says, I hope you take it. I said, well, I will take it. Earl Crumb was leader then at that point. Yeah, he was the manager. He was the leader. He wasn't the leader, he was the manager. The manager. It was his. We rehearsed without a drum. Because they didn't do too much reading. In fact I think I was about the best reader in the band. In fact I'm pretty sure of that.
